extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians / computational number theorists working on lattice-based searches for large values of arithmetic sums (Mertens function, related h_P and h_StR functions)
extracted.subtask_description: Design and run lattice-based enumeration experiments to find x (via an auxiliary parameter y) that maximize or minimize arithmetic test functions (h_P or h_StR), choosing lattice construction, reduction and enumeration parameters, and computational precision to make the search feasible and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of N (dimension) vs available computational power
rubrics_metrics.description: N is 'the bigger the better', but the only constraint is the amount of computational power available. In experiments N∈{120,130,140}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher N improves the search but increases time and memory; try several large values (e.g. 120–140) and pick the best candidate empirically. Larger N may not always give better candidates in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling factor γ (controls candidate count)
rubrics_metrics.description: γ≥1 is a parameter that controls the number of candidate points to be enumerated since |L ∩ Ball_n(t,K)| ≈ γ^{N+1}. In experiments γ∈[1,1.28] (examples: γ=1.19,1.23,1.25,1.28).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose γ modestly above 1 (e.g. 1.19–1.25) to keep enumeration feasible; larger γ explodes the Gaussian-heuristic candidate count. Use γ together with reduction/pruning so actual enumerated points remain tractable (experiment logs show far fewer enumerated points than the heuristic count).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameters ν, ν_y, ν_t — relative sizes and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The parameters ν, ν_y, ν_t strongly influence the entry sizes of the lattice (3.3). Heuristics suggest ν−ν_t needs to be at least comparable to N to make certain quantities small; ν_t must not be too small (previous constructions with ν_t=0 were problematic). If ν is large, ν_y must be of comparable size to ν for (3.7) to be reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select ν,ν_y,ν_t to balance entry sizes and maintain efficiency: in experiments choices like ν=130, ν_y=100, ν_t between 12 and 30 worked well. Avoid ν_t too small; ensure ν−ν_t ~ O(N) for favorable scaling in (3.6). If increasing ν, adjust ν_y and ν_t accordingly — there is a 'sweet spot' found empirically by trial and error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle unbalanced lattice and avoid enumerating trivial translates
rubrics_metrics.description: When ν≫ν_y the lattice defined by (3.2) is unbalanced: the top row has norm much smaller than det(L)^{1/(N+1)}, so many integer translates u + m b1 lie in the ball. Therefore enumeration should avoid returning all lattice points corresponding to such translates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerate points in the projection of L onto the hyperplane orthogonal to b1 (Alg.1 variant) to avoid enumerating O(ℤ⋅b1) translates. Practically, filter enumerated u so there is no nonzero m∈ℤ with ||t−u−m b1|| < ||t−u||.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use progressive 1‑round BKZ reduction (LLL then BKZ tours)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute a progressive 1-round BKZ reduced basis by running LLL, then one tour of BKZ-20, BKZ-21, ..., up to a target (examples given: BKZ-83 or BKZ-88).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fplll to perform LLL followed by incremental BKZ tours up to the desired blocksize (e.g. BKZ-83 or BKZ-88) to obtain a well-reduced basis before enumeration. This often takes a few hours on a single core for N≈120–140.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pruned enumeration (variant of LN13) with suitable pruning/scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: Run pruned enumeration (Alg.1, variant of LN13) with chosen scaling factor radius γ and target t'; examples: γ=1.23 gave 37,937 lattice points (≈2 days single core), γ=1.19 gave 17,406 points (few hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tune pruning and scaling (γ) to balance runtime and coverage. Monitor actual enumerated counts (much smaller than Gaussian heuristic) and adjust γ or pruning to keep runtimes to a few core‑days. Expect that each enumerated projected point may correspond to many translates (accounted for by projection strategy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Software and numeric precision requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Arb for guaranteed interval arithmetic to compute h_P and h_StR; fplll for basis reduction (LLL/BKZ); NTL for implementation of pruned enumeration. Zeta zeros up to height 14,000 were used with Hurst data computed to ≈10,000 decimal digits; for heights up to 74,000 Arb with ≈300 decimal digits sufficed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose high-precision arithmetic appropriate to the height of zeros and the function being computed (10,000 digits for lower heights, ≈300 digits for higher ranges when using Arb). Plan runtime: some computations took less than a core day; others (enumeration) took a few core-days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use heuristics (3.6) and (3.7) to predict ranges for components and y
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristics predict sqrt(α_i^*)|γ_i y − ψ_i|_{2π} ∈ 2^{-3.6−(ν−ν_t)/(N+1)}⋅[1,γ] for each i, and y ∈ 2^{-3.6 + ν_y − ν_t − (ν−ν_t)/(N+1)}⋅[1,γ]. These serve as guides to where good y values lie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these heuristics 'with a grain of salt' — they give useful search intervals and in experiments y values fell within a factor 2^4 of the heuristic predictions. Use them to set search ranges and pruning radii.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerate a ball of appropriate radius — not too large
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumeration should be over a ball (center t, radius R ≈ K), but the radius must not be too large: maxima of h_StR(y) are not necessarily the closest lattice points, but h_P(y)>1 seems unlikely when the distance is beyond a threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose radius close to the predicted K (K depends on γ, det L, N, ν, ν_t etc). Empirically enumerate a ball large enough to find candidates but small enough to avoid excessive unrelated points; use correlation plots (as in paper) to set a sensible threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on partial sums with largest weights α_i^*
rubrics_metrics.description: When checking the soundness of approximations, restrict to the partial sum terms with largest α_i^*; high (resp. low) values of h_StR are found among high (resp. low) values of this partial sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the partial sum on the lattice terms (largest α_i^*) to guide the search — it correlates with the full function and lets you prioritize promising lattice points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation criterion for candidate y (target function magnitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: We seek y for which |h_P(y)| or |h_StR(y)| exceeds 1 (or is large in magnitude); tables report y values where h_P(y)≈−1.012, h_StR(y)≈−1.007, and near-misses slightly below/above 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the target function h_P or h_StR reliably using high-precision arithmetic; track near-misses and keep candidates with values >1 (or close to critical thresholds). Slight perturbations of y can sometimes improve the value (see perturbation example given by referee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perturbation and refinement of found y
rubrics_metrics.description: Slight perturbations of a found y can improve the target function (example: a tiny change in decimal expansion improved h_StR from −1.007 to ≈−1.001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After finding a promising candidate, perform small local perturbations (and recompute with adequate precision) to refine y and potentially improve the target function. Also consider using refined theoretical bounds (e.g. for fraktur_x) to tighten conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of scaling pitfalls from integer flooring effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between x⋅⌊α⌋ and ⌊x⋅α⌋ can scale with x; this can make expectations (like (3.5)) diverge from heuristics if ν_t is too small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure ν_t not too small to prevent large scaling errors; account for floor effects when estimating how discretization impacts sums and distances. Prior constructions fixing ν_t=0 were problematic for this reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance parameter trade-offs empirically (no closed-form optimum)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are trade-offs when tuning parameters (e.g. increasing ν may require increasing ν_y, which may break ν≫ν_y condition crucial for efficiency). The paper suggests these must be determined by trial and error; there may be a 'sweet spot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform systematic experiments varying N, ν, ν_y, ν_t, γ, reduction blocksize and pruning to find best empirical performance; monitor both enumeration counts and final target function values to guide tuning.
